questions.q: What compiler is used to build a CUDA C++ (.cu) file?
options: gcc
nvcc
clang
python
questions.explain: nvcc is NVIDIA's CUDA compiler, which handles both the ordinary host C++ code and the device kernel code within the same .cu file.

questions.q: Why is vector addition considered the canonical first CUDA example?
options: It is the most computationally intensive operation possible on a GPU
It exercises the full host/device/kernel/launch pattern with minimal algorithmic complexity
It requires no memory allocation at all
It is the only operation that can use shared memory
questions.explain: Vector addition is genuinely parallel but algorithmically trivial, so it demonstrates the full CUDA program structure (allocate, copy, launch, copy back, free) without extra complexity getting in the way.

questions.q: Why do CUDA programs need to explicitly check for errors with cudaGetLastError()?
options: Because CUDA calls throw C++ exceptions that must be caught
Because a kernel launch doesn't return a value you can inspect directly, so it can fail silently without an explicit check
Because cudaGetLastError() is required before every cudaMalloc call
Because the GPU driver crashes on any error without this check
questions.explain: CUDA calls don't throw exceptions; a kernel launch itself gives no direct feedback, so an error can go unnoticed unless you explicitly call cudaGetLastError() to retrieve it.

questions.q: In the vectorAdd example, what does the line `int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;` accomplish?
options: It allocates global memory for the result array
It computes the thread's global index so each thread works on a unique array element
It launches the kernel
It synchronizes all threads in the block
questions.explain: This is the global index formula from lesson 7, converting a thread's block and in-block position into a single index used to access the correct array element.

questions.q: What makes vector addition a low-arithmetic-intensity, memory-bound operation?
options: It performs many floating-point operations per byte of data moved
It performs only one addition per two reads and one write — very little compute relative to the data moved
It uses only registers and no global memory
It requires double-precision floating point
questions.explain: Vector addition does one add operation for every two values read and one value written, which is a very low ratio of compute to data movement — making it memory-bound rather than compute-bound.
